title: Pins
subtitle: Freeze a piece against something more valuable behind it.
goals: Attack pinned pieces to win them

steps.say: A pin freezes an enemy piece against something more valuable behind it on the same line. If the piece behind is the KING, the pin is 'absolute' — the pinned piece literally cannot move. Pinned pieces are paralyzed pieces: attack them, ignore them, walk right past them.

steps.prompt: Black's d-pawn is gone — the diagonal to the king lies open. Pin the c6 knight!
hints: Find the diagonal running from your bishop's reach through c6 to e8.
A bishop on b5 lines up: bishop, knight... king. Absolute pin.

line.say: Absolute pin! With d7 empty, the knight stands directly between your bishop and the king — it cannot legally move at all. A frozen piece.

rejections.say: Strong development toward f7 — but it pins nothing. The task: freeze that c6 knight against its king.
Modest and pin-free. Look one diagonal further — through c6, all the way to e8.

steps.wrongSay: Line up bishop → knight → king on one diagonal.
steps.successSay: Absolute pins turn pieces into statues. Now let's learn to punish statues.

steps.prompt: The c6 knight is pinned — so ATTACK it! Pinned pieces can't run away.
hints: The golden rule: pile attackers onto a pinned piece. What's the cheapest attacker you have?
Push the d-pawn one square — the frozen knight can only watch it come.

line.say: The pawn marches straight at the paralyzed knight — it cannot flee!
Black broke the pin a move too late — the knight never escaped. A whole piece for a pawn.

rejections.say: bxc6 — you traded your beautiful pinning bishop for the knight. Even trade, pin gone. Attacking the pinned piece with a PAWN wins it outright.

steps.wrongSay: The knight is frozen — attack it with something it can't answer. Your cheapest unit is ideal.
steps.successSay: Pin, then pile on — cheapest attacker first. That two-step recipe wins pieces for pawns.

steps.prompt: The c6 knight 'defends' e5... or does it? Win a pawn!
hints: A pinned piece is a fake defender — it can't actually recapture.
Take the e5 pawn and dare the knight to do something about it.

line.say: Free pawn! Nxe5 by Black is illegal — the knight is absolutely pinned to the king. Its 'defense' of e5 was pure theater.

rejections.say: It wins the e5 pawn eventually too — but why surrender the bishop pair? Nxe5 pockets the pawn immediately and KEEPS the pin working.

steps.wrongSay: Count e5's defenders again — does a pinned knight really count?
steps.successSay: Pinned pieces defend nothing. Recount every 'defended' pawn once a pin appears.

steps.prompt: Black's bishop 'pins' your e5 knight to the queen. Prove the pin is FAKE — the legendary sacrifice!
hints: The pin against a QUEEN is only relative — the knight CAN move, if the consequences favor you. What happens after Nxe5 Bxd1?
Calculate: Nxe5, Bxd1, Bxf7+, Ke7 — and now a quiet knight hop delivers mate. The queen was never really lost, and Black's king is.

line.say: The knight breaks the 'pin' — offering the queen!
LEGALL'S MATE! Three minor pieces weave a net the queen could never have escaped. The pin was fake because mate outweighs a queen.

rejections.say: A polite question to the bishop — but you're sitting on one of the most famous combinations in chess history. The 'pin' is fake: Nxe5! and if Bxd1, mate follows in two.
Breaking the pin voluntarily — safe, but you had Legall's immortal Nxe5! sacrifice. Relative pins are promises, not prisons.

steps.wrongSay: The knight is pinned to your QUEEN, not your king. When does a queen sacrifice pay off? Calculate Nxe5!
steps.successSay: Legall's Mate (Paris, ~1750) — the eternal reminder that relative pins can be broken when checkmate is on the table.
